chunk_findings.detail: The checklist says `ddflow adopt --agents cline` “writes rules only” because Cline’s MCP settings are one global file and there is no project file to write. The next step then tells the reader to copy the `ddflow` server launch line “from the launch line in any adopted project’s `.mcp.json`.” A first-time Cline user following this in a throwaway repo where only Cline was adopted will have no `.mcp.json`, because the previous step explicitly says none is created, so the Approve step cannot be done from the documented source.

chunk_findings.detail: `new = "6"` is a TOML string, but `hooks.fixture_max_age_months` is a numeric setting (“this many whole months”). When the upgrade machinery applies this template, it will write the value as the string `"6"` into the config. A later consumer that parses this knob as an integer (for age comparison in `ddflow harness record` or the fixture gap report) then either fails config validation or raises `TypeError` comparing `str` and `int`. It should be `new = 6` in TOML.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.hooks.fixture_max_age_months.toml:6

chunk_findings.detail: The recorded UserPromptSubmit hook command wraps its launcher paths in double quotes, e.g. `[ -x "[REDACTED:path]" ]` and `PYTHONPATH="[REDACTED:path]"`. In sh/bash, tilde expansion is suppressed inside double quotes, so the path is interpreted as a literal `~` directory under the current working directory rather than the user's home. On a machine where ddflow is only installed at the recorded launcher path and is not on PATH, the first branch is never taken, `command -v ddflow` fails, and the hook emits `ddflow: not found...` instead of running. Since this fixture is supposed to capture what `ddflow adopt` wrote, tests consuming it will bless a generated hook that silently skips local-only installs.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/harness/claude/session/adopt.json:45

chunk_findings.detail: The `tools/list` pair’s `result.tools` is an array of plain strings (`"ddflow_brief"`, …, `"ddflow_view"`) instead of MCP Tool objects with `name`, `description`, and `inputSchema`. Since the fixture is recorded “live MCP traffic through the tap,” replaying this pair against a compliant MCP client or running conformance checks that validate tool schemas will reject it as invalid MCP data, making the fixture fail to faithfully represent a real session.

chunk_findings.detail: The `"compact_summary"` value is a double-quoted JSON string, but it contains many unescaped double-quote characters inside it, e.g. `... prompt "Reply with the single word PONG and nothing else", then ...` and `"PONG"`, `"DONE"`. That makes the fixture invalid JSON: the first inner `"` terminates the string and the parser fails. Any test that loads this fixture with a JSON parser (`tests/test_harness_fixtures.py` is part of this change and loads the fixture files) will hit `json.JSONDecodeError` before the harness recorder logic runs, so the new conformance test fails on this input.

chunk_findings.detail: The `PreCompact` stdin payload includes `"prompt_id": "b12ae6be-5f0c-4687-9a33-6681ac070e94"`. Claude Code’s actual `PreCompact` hook input contains `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `trigger`, and `custom_instructions`, but no `prompt_id`. Because this fixture is marked `"recorded": true` and used as a live recording, a harness tap that assumes every hook payload has a `prompt_id` will pass against this fixture and then crash with a `KeyError` on a real PreCompact event. The fixture should omit `prompt_id` to match the real hook schema.

chunk_findings.detail: `mcp()` calls `McpLog(capture)` before spawning the real server, and `McpLog.__init__` performs `capture.mkdir(...)` and `os.open(capture / MCP_LOG, ...)` with no try/except. If the capture path is not writable (for example `/proc/1/capture` or a read-only filesystem), `McpLog(capture)` raises `PermissionError`, propagates uncaught through `main`, and the command exits nonzero without ever running the MCP server. That violates the module's own load-bearing property that a tap that cannot store still passes bytes and exits 0.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness_tap.py:106

chunk_findings.detail: `hook()` reads exactly `stdin.read(MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES)` and then returns, leaving the rest of stdin unread. For any payload longer than 1 MiB (the exact case the limit exists for), the hook process exits while the writer may still be writing; an agent harness that writes the hook payload through a pipe and does not suppress `EPIPE`/`SIGPIPE` can fail the observed turn. The process should consume all stdin, storing at most `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES`, rather than closing the read end early.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness_tap.py:57

chunk_findings.detail: `rows` globs only `fixtures.glob("*.json")` and `fixtures.glob(f"{SESSION_DIR}/*.json")`. But committed fixtures for a harness include `unmapped/*.json` files (the manifest lists `tests/fixtures/harness/claude/unmapped/{post_compact,subagent_start,subagent_stop,subagent_stop_compaction}.json`). Given an `unmapped/post_compact.json` with a stale `_meta.date`, `rows` omits it entirely from the table/report, so it is never flagged as stale, contrary to the function’s doc “Every committed fixture of one agent”.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness_record.py:rows

chunk_findings.detail: `_pairs` is documented as producing pairs “in the order they were asked”, but it appends each pair when its response is logged, not when its request was logged. Given log rows with `in id=1`, `in id=2`, `out id=2`, `out id=1`, the returned list is `[id=2, id=1]`, not ask order. If the replayed `session/mcp.json` pairs are consumed in list order, this interleaving changes the order in the fixture.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness_record.py:_pairs

chunk_findings.detail: `hook` calls `stdin.read(MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES)` exactly once and then exits. When the tap is run as a subprocess, its stdin is a pipe, and a single pipe read is not required to return the full payload before returning; it can return as soon as some bytes are available. A hook payload larger than one pipe chunk (e.g. a 200 KiB prompt payload written through a subprocess pipe) can therefore be stored as only the first chunk and the tap exits 0, leaving the stored JSON truncated below `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES`. The leftover writer of the pipe can then see `EPIPE` despite the tap exiting 0. This violates the module’s stated “It never fails the turn it observes” property and can make recorded fixtures incomplete or marked stale.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness_tap.py:53 (`hook`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `record` subcommand does not add the `--run` consent flag that the immediately preceding harness subparser uses to gate execution of `<binary> --version` (“the operator consents: run `<binary> --version`”). The record parser’s own `--agent-version` help says the version is “asked of its binary when [detect] names one”, so `ddflow harness record claude --prepare /tmp/scratch` can run the detected agent binary without the operator passing any consent flag; this violates the surrounding harness CLI’s consent gate for running that binary.

chunk_findings.detail: `Scrubber.text` replaces registered session ids before the project/home literals. If a session id is a substring of the project root, replacing it first stops the later root literal from matching, so the root is left partially scrubbed and `leaks` cannot detect it. Concrete input: root `/work/a1b2c3d4/proj`, home `[REDACTED:path]`, capture payload has `session_id = "a1b2c3d4"`, and a string contains `/work/a1b2c3d4/proj/file.txt`. `text` turns that string into `/work/s-1/proj/file.txt`; `leaks` then searches the dumped JSON for the original `/work/a1b2c3d4/proj`, finds nothing, and reports no project-path leak. chunk_findings.detail: `main` now ends a successful MCP tap with `os._exit(mcp(...))`, which skips Python's file-close flush. `McpLog.note` only `write`s the JSON line into an `os.fdopen(..., "ab")` buffer and never `flush`es. chunk_findings.detail: `_pump` treats `BrokenPipeError` as “session over” and returns, but only closes `dst`. In `mcp`, the outbound pump’s `dst` is `sys.stdout.buffer` and `src` is the MCP child’s stdout. If the agent dies or closes its read end while the child is still writing, that write raises, the pump stops reading, and `mcp` then blocks in `child.wait()`. The child fills the unread stdout pipe and blocks on its next write, so both sides hang: given a child that keeps emitting stdout and an agent that closes the tap’s stdout, `harness_tap` never exits and the server never gets SIGPIPE or a closed stdin.

chunk_findings.detail: `_scrubber()` uses home `[REDACTED:path]` and project root `/tmp/x.y/z`, and this file’s other assertions treat `~` as home and `/w`/`-w` as the project (`transcript_path` becomes `[REDACTED:path]`, key `/tmp/x.y/z/f` becomes `/w/f`). Given input `x/-home-me-.claude/y`, which encodes only the home directory and not the project, the test requires `x/-w-.claude/y`. chunk_findings.detail: The reorder stores the first chunk before the drainage loop, so when `store_hook` raises `OSError` — e.g. the capture directory is unwritable or the disk is full — the outer `except OSError` exits without consuming the rest of stdin. That closes the pipe while the producer/agent may still be writing the payload, which the code’s own `while` comment says can make the agent fail. The old order drained stdin before calling `store_hook`, so a storage error still returned 0 only after all input had been consumed; the new code regresses that guarantee in the failure path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness_tap.py:hook

chunk_findings.detail: The new `STOP_GRACE_S` timeout is only reached after `_pump(child.stdout, sys.stdout.buffer, log, "out")` returns. If the agent closes the tap stdout read end and the MCP child hangs without writing anything (e.g. a child in `sleep(10**6)` with stdout open, ignoring EOF on stdin), `_pump` remains blocked in reading `child.stdout`; no write to `sys.stdout.buffer` occurs, so no `BrokenPipeError` is raised and `_pump` never returns. `mcp` therefore never reaches `child.wait(timeout=STOP_GRACE_S)` and never calls `proc.stop_group`, so the tap process hangs indefinitely. The new test only covers a child that keeps producing output; a quiet non-exiting child still leaves the same cleanup hang.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness_tap.py:mcp

chunk_findings.detail: Moving `store_hook` ahead of the drain loop, still inside the same `try`, skips the drain when storing fails. Given a hook payload larger than `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` and `store_hook` raising `OSError` (capture dir not writable, disk full), the handler prints and returns 0 without the `while stdin.read(...)` loop. The unread tail stays in the pipe; when the tap then exits, the agent’s next write gets `SIGPIPE`/`BrokenPipeError`. The old order consumed stdin before `store_hook`, which is what the “agent may fail on a pipe closed under it” loop is there to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: `hook` calls `stdin.read(MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES)` exactly once and then exits. When the tap is run as a subprocess, its stdin is a pipe, and a single pipe read is not required to return the full payload before returning; it can return as soon as some bytes are available. A hook payload larger than one pipe chunk (e.g. a 200 KiB prompt payload written through a subprocess pipe) can therefore be stored as only the first chunk and the tap exits 0, leaving the stored JSON truncated below `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES`. The leftover writer of the pipe can then see `EPIPE` despite the tap exiting 0. This violates the module’s stated “It never fails the turn it observes” property and can make recorded fixtures incomplete or marked stale.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite to `os._exit(mcp(...))` bypasses Python’s normal interpreter shutdown, so the `BufferedWriter` created by `os.fdopen(fd, "ab")` for `McpLog._f` is never flushed. `McpLog.note` writes each row to that buffered writer with no explicit `flush`, and a captured MCP session that emits less than the 8 KiB buffer (or the trailing partial buffer of a larger session) leaves those rows only in process memory when `mcp` returns and `os._exit` terminates. The recorded `mcp.jsonl` is then missing rows, making the fixture incomplete and breaking replay/stale-row consumers. Concrete example: `ddflow services.harness_tap mcp /tmp/capture -- python -c 'print("{\"d\":\"out\",\"line\":\"hi\"}"); exit(0)'` exits via `os._exit` before the buffered line is written, so the file has no `"hi"` row.

chunk_findings.detail: `main` now ends a successful MCP tap with `os._exit(mcp(...))`, which skips Python's file-close flush. `McpLog.note` only `write`s the JSON line into an `os.fdopen(..., "ab")` buffer and never `flush`es. A short session (one `tools/list` plus a reply, a few hundred bytes, under the default 8 KiB buffer) therefore returns from `mcp()` with the log still in memory; `_exit` drops it and `mcp.jsonl` stays empty or short. Before this change a normal return closed the fd and flushed. The comment that everything is already written is false for that input.

chunk_findings.detail: `hook` is documented as always returning 0, and the previous `try` wrapped both the payload read and the drain. chunk_findings.detail: `Scrubber.text` replaces registered session ids before the project/home literals. If a session id is a substring of the project root, replacing it first stops the later root literal from matching, so the root is left partially scrubbed and `leaks` cannot detect it. Concrete input: root `/work/a1b2c3d4/proj`, home `[REDACTED:path]`, capture payload has `session_id = "a1b2c3d4"`, and a string contains `/work/a1b2c3d4/proj/file.txt`. `text` turns that string into `/work/s-1/proj/file.txt`; `leaks` then searches the dumped JSON for the original `/work/a1b2c3d4/proj`, finds nothing, and reports no project-path leak. The public fixture still exposes this machine's directory structure, violating the scrub-and-refuse guarantee.
